note:
Someone commissioned directly by Christ as His authoritative messenger (2 Cor. 1:1 note). Paul explains the significance of this office elsewhere (ch. 9; 15:1–11; 2 Cor. 10–12; Gal. 1). Some of the problems in the Corinthian church that Paul addresses involve challenges to his authority.

**Sosthenes.** Perhaps the same person mentioned in Acts 18:17, ruler of the synagogue in Corinth at the time of Paul’s first visit to the city.

The word “saints” (lit. “holy ones”) calls attention to the distinctive status of God’s people as those set apart by God for Himself. Paul often uses it to identify the Christians to whom he writes (e.g., Rom. 1:7). The description “sanctified” underlines this reality of the Christian life. The Corinthians were plagued by ethical problems and this letter touches repeatedly on the subject of holiness. Significantly, however, Paul encourages them here in a pastoral way by reminding them that by God’s grace they have already made a definitive break with sin and now serve the Lord Jesus Christ (6:11). The goal of progressive holiness is realistic because God has already changed their hearts (Rom. 6:1–14; Gal. 5:24, 25).

verse_quote: in every way you were enriched.
note: The Corinthians were tempted to become puffed up by their gifts of “knowledge” and of speaking “in tongues” (8:1; 14:23). Paul needs to rebuke them for their self-centered and loveless misuse of those gifts (12:14–26; 13:1–3, 9–13; 14:4–5), but he does not deny or minimize the spiritual gifts they have received (v. 7).

Paul encourages his readers by assuring them that God, who began a work of grace in them, can be trusted to complete it. Indeed, they will be presented “guiltless” at the time of Christ’s return. Note the similarities between vv. 8, 9 and Phil. 1:6, 10 (cf. Eph. 5:26, 27; 1 Thess. 5:23, 24).

This exhortation begins the body of the letter and announces Paul’s primary concern. He has heard (vv. 11, 12) that the unity of the Corinthian church has broken down. Many of the problems addressed in this letter (parties, lawsuits, tensions between “strong” and “weak,” indifference to the poor at the Lord’s Supper, boasting about spiritual gifts) reflect the spirit of dissension that was in the community.
Chloe must have been an influential Christian, perhaps a member of the Corinthian church, although she is not mentioned elsewhere.

An effective preacher from Alexandria who had ministered in Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24–19:1). Paul will stress that he and Apollos have distinct and complementary ministries as servants privileged to co-labor with God (3:5–15). Paul’s later report that he had urged Apollos to return to Corinth (16:12) shows their respective parties that he and Apollos did not view each other as rivals, but enjoyed mutual respect and unity.

**Cephas.** The Aramaic name (meaning “rock,” as does the Gk. _petros_) given by Jesus to Simon Peter (John 1:42). Paul acknowledged that Peter was regarded as among the “pillars” of the church (Gal. 2:8–9). Peter’s prominence in the dissemination of the gospel is evident in the book of Acts. He was obviously popular among some groups in Corinth (perhaps the Jewish Christians), but it is unclear whether he had actually visited the church.

With this question, Paul anticipates one of his fundamental teachings about the church. Just as a physical body, though made up of many members, is one, so also the church, which is the body of Christ, cannot be divided (10:16, 17; 12:12 note).

The facts that Paul did not invoke his own name in baptizing but that of Christ (v. 13; Acts 2:38) and that he personally baptized few in Corinth (see v. 16) show that the apostle had no interest in enlisting a group of devotees for himself.

**Crispus.** The synagogue ruler whose conversion is recorded in Acts 18:8.

**Gaius.** A common name. Perhaps this is the Gaius described in Acts 19:29.

Paul’s first converts in Corinth, respected for their dedication. Stephanas himself was one of the representatives who brought a communication from the Corinthians to Paul (16:15–17). See theological note “Infant Baptism” on p. 41.

verse_quote: not with words of eloquent wisdom.
note:
The Corinthian church had an unhealthy regard for rhetorical display. Paul will focus attention on what true wisdom is (1:18–2:16; 3:18–23). In this verse, he reminds the Corinthians that the power of his own preaching in Corinth did not depend on such skills (2:1–5).

**cross of Christ.** In the opinion of those who are wise according to this world, proclaiming the crucified Lord is foolishness. Paul therefore treats “wisdom” and “the cross” as opposites (v. 23 note).

According to the Bible, there will be two types of response to the gospel arising from God’s elective purpose (Is. 6:9, 10; Luke 2:34; Rom. 9:10–13; 2 Cor. 2:15, 16; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). This truth does not make God responsible for the perishing of unbelievers; they perish because of their own sin and stubborn impenitence. Those who believe and are saved, on the other hand, are “those who are called” (v. 24; cf. Rom. 9:16).

It is not clear whether Paul intends a sharp distinction between these three categories. Possibly the first is general in character, while the other two are specifically Jewish scribes and Greek teachers.

**this age ... the world.** Much of Paul’s theology is built on the basic opposition between “the present evil age” (Gal. 1:4), or world, which is characterized by “the flesh” (human nature under the adverse effects of the fall), and the coming age of life and blessing, which has already dawned for those who have received the Spirit (10:11; Gal. 5:16, 17; Eph. 1:13, 14; 2:6; Phil. 3:20).

verse_quote: the folly of what we preach.
note: This passage is filled with intense irony. Those who are wise according to the standards of the world think the gospel is foolish, since it identifies one who has suffered shameful crucifixion as the unique and only remedy to the plight of humanity. But even the most “foolish” thing about God is wiser than human wisdom (vv. 25, 27). God can use the simplicity and seeming shamefulness of the gospel’s central event, the cross, to demonstrate that real foolishness belongs to those who oppose Him (v. 27). The arrogance of human wisdom blinds unbelievers to the truth. Jesus thanked the Father for His good pleasure in hiding these things from the wise and learned but revealing them to little children (Matt. 11:25, 26).

Paul identifies precisely what the world finds offensive about the gospel (cf. v. 17; 2:2). Possibly these words also reflect the reason for Paul’s opposition to the gospel before his conversion. The thought that the Messiah (God’s anointed) had been hanged on a tree and thereby came under the divine curse (Gal. 3:13; Deut. 21:23) was intolerable to many Jews.

verse_quote: Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
note: God’s wisdom and power are not abstract forces but personal qualities that manifest themselves fully in the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ (v. 30; Rom. 1:4, 16; Col. 2:1–3).

Salvation, by its very nature, does not depend on human values or achievement. Even those in the Corinthian church who might have been justly admired could not have claimed that they were chosen because of any good in them. Rather, God has mercy on all who acknowledge their sinfulness (Mark 2:17; John 9:39–41). See theological note “Effectual Calling” on p. 2146.

**not many were wise ... powerful ... of noble birth.** God’s election is not contingent or conditioned on qualities that He discerns in those whom He chooses. Moses reminded the Israelites that God had chosen them despite the fact that as a people they were both few (Deut. 7:6–8) and rebellious (Deut. 9:4–6). Likewise, most of the believers in Corinth lacked the wisdom prized by Greeks, the power admired by Romans (and Jews), and the pedigree admired by Greeks, Romans, and Jews. They had also been lacking in ethical purity until God’s grace washed and sanctified them in Christ (6:9–11).

verse_quote: no human being might boast in the presence of God.
note: This principle, which Paul underscores in v. 31 by quoting Jer. 9:24, provides the foundation for the biblical doctrine of salvation: it is a gracious gift from God that rules out human boasting (Eph. 2:8, 9).

verse_quote: who became to us wisdom from God.
note: See note on v. 24. Paul explains how Jesus is “wisdom” to the believer. He is “our righteousness,” by which we are justified (Rom. 3:21–26); He is “our sanctification”—the one by whose grace we are set apart to God (1:2) and progressively renewed (Rom. 6:1–23); He is “our redemption”—the one whose death and resurrection ensures that we, soul and body will be fully redeemed from sin’s guilt (Eph. 1:7) and its penalty, death (Rom. 8:23).

Paul must be referring to his first visit to Corinth, recorded in Acts 18:1–17 (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**with lofty speech or wisdom.** Influenced by Greek culture, some of the Christians in Corinth may have been critical of Paul for not using the rhetorical techniques of their contemporaries (2 Cor. 11:5, 6). See notes on 4:1, 8–13; 9:3, 19; 10:30; 16:3.
See note on 1:23. Paul here identifies the substance of his preaching (Gal. 3:1; 1 Cor. 15:1ff.).

Taken by themselves, these verses might suggest that Paul was timid, uneducated, and unable to speak with force and eloquence. Both the book of Acts (e.g., 19:8) and Paul’s own letters (ch. 13) prove otherwise. Yet some found Paul’s oral delivery to fall short of the standards of Greek rhetoric (2 Cor. 10:10) and his personal appearance to be unattractive (2 Cor. 10:10; cf. Gal. 4:12–15). “Self-confidence,” if it rests on arrogance concerning one’s own strength, reflects a desire to be independent from God. Paul had learned that God can use human weakness to show forth His own glory (2 Cor. 12:7–10). Because he knew that men and women will be convinced by the gospel only “in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,” Paul used his talents and training with a full and proper confidence in God, rather than relying on his own skills.

Lit. “perfect.” The apostle does not have in mind a special category of elite Christians, an idea that may have been present among the Corinthians. Paul may be taking a term in use by the Corinthians and assigning it its proper meaning (see Phil. 3:15). Paul’s expression here is no doubt equivalent to “spiritual” (vv. 13, 15; 3:1), referring to the influence of the Holy Spirit. The mature or spiritual person is the person in whom the Holy Spirit dwells and whose life the Holy Spirit directs (cf. v. 14). Since every true believer has received the Spirit, every believer is spiritual and can understand God’s wisdom, the gospel of Jesus Christ.

**we do impart wisdom.** The gospel, the proclamation of Christ crucified. Throughout this section (vv. 6–16), the “we” for whom Paul speaks are primarily the apostles, who receive revelation by the Spirit (v. 10) and speak it in Spirit-taught words (v. 13). Yet every believer has received God’s Spirit and has thereby been enlightened to receive the apostolic message, which has been set into writing in the New Testament so that the church may have it in the post-apostolic age.

verse_quote: a secret and hidden wisdom of God.
note:
This passage should not be interpreted as a reference to mysteries accessible only to superior Christians. The riches of the gospel, though “hidden” during the OT period, have now been revealed by the Spirit (v. 10). Eph. 3:2–6 makes plain that the word “mystery” has a strong temporal meaning. The “mystery” is a truth that “was not made known ... in other generations” (Eph. 3:5); it was “kept secret for long ages” (Rom. 16:25). But now the truth has been clearly revealed to all those who have the Spirit, who live in “the end of the ages” (10:11). The “mystery” (_mysterion_) is something partially hidden in the OT that is now revealed in the NT as an end-time reality. (The word “mystery” occurs in the Septuagint only in Daniel 2 [e.g., 2:28–29] as a latter-day idea associated with the establishment of God’s kingdom on earth.) At least part of the mystery here is that the Messiah suffers as “the Lord of glory,” but the NT more clearly reveals that the Messiah is the glorious Lord God _in the midst of_ suffering, reigning _at the same time_ that He seems to be defeated by Satan on the cross and while He is bearing the divine curse on sin (“Lord” is the translation of the covenant name Yahweh in the OT, which is now applied to Jesus). It is this that “the rulers of this age” did not “understand.”

**decreed.** The word is used also in Rom. 8:29, 30 and Eph. 1:5 to express the certainty of God’s goodwill for His people.

verse_quote: None of the rulers of this age understood.
note:
Unbelievers are still part of the old age and so have not received God’s wisdom (v. 14). Paul emphasizes this point by focusing on the most influential members of society (1:20). The rulers’ ignorance of God’s mysterious plan did not excuse their crime (cf. Luke 23:34).

**crucified the Lord of glory.** Although the incarnate Son of God suffered crucifixion with respect to His human nature, the unity of His two natures, divine and human, in one person makes it fitting for Paul to associate Christ’s divine title “Lord of glory” with His human vulnerability to the anguish of death. See note on Acts 20:28.

In contrast to the wise of this world (who cannot even conceive of the greatness of divine salvation), those who love God both perceive and experience His blessings. The quotation is based on Is. 64:4, but it includes other ideas found in the OT.

See theological note “The Illumination of the Holy Spirit.”

**searches everything.** The idea of divine searching (cf. Ps. 139:1; Rom. 8:27) emphasizes God’s omniscience, particularly His power to see what is invisible to humans (John 2:25). It does not imply that the Holy Spirit needs to seek knowledge of the Father that He otherwise lacks. The Spirit probes the depths of divine knowledge for our benefit.

This verse intends to make a common-sense observation, not to give an analysis of human personality. “Spirit” refers generally to the immaterial part of a human being, especially human mental faculties (v. 16 note).

verse_quote: interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
note: The precise meaning of this clause is disputed. As the text note suggests, Paul may be restating and combining the points of vv. 10 and 13: as an apostle, Paul speaks the content revealed by the Spirit in the words given to him by the Spirit (2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:20–21). Probably Paul had been criticized in Corinth for not using human eloquence and wisdom (v. 1 note). In reply, he says that the truths revealed by the Spirit must be explained in a way that is harmonious with the Spirit.

The “natural” person, who still belongs to the old age, is contrasted with the one who is “spiritual,” that is, one who is united to Christ, indwelt by His Spirit, and therefore belongs to the age to come. Note Nicodemus’ confusion when Jesus speaks of being born from above by the Spirit (John 3:1–12).
The apostle may be responding to individuals who opposed him and passed negative judgments on him (v. 1 note).

Through the Spirit of the Lord, Paul has the mind of Christ, and therefore the mind of the Lord. Those opponents who do not see that the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of the Lord are one and the same have no warrant to instruct or examine him. By implication, those who accept Paul’s teaching have the blessing of the Spirit and understand the things of God. Paul probably alludes to Is. 40:13, which associates the infinity of God’s Spirit with His boundless wisdom and knowledge (cf. Rom. 11:34).

That is, belonging to the Holy Spirit (2:6 note).

**people of the flesh.** “Flesh” is Paul’s main word for describing the present evil age. Since the Corin­thians had received the Holy Spirit, they were spiritual in the most fundamental sense, but their behavior was so inconsistent with that truth that Paul had to treat them as people who had little understanding of what it means to think and live as those who belong to the new age.
See note on 1:10. These behaviors characterize life in the flesh, or this present evil age (cf. the works of the flesh in contrast to the fruit of the Spirit in Gal. 5:19–23).

Paul’s aim was to preach the gospel in places where the message of Christ had not been heard (Rom. 15:20).

**Apollos.** See note on 1:12.

Paul may mean either that Christian workers are co-laborers with God or that Christians who are co-laborers with one another belong to God. Paul’s point is clear from the context: God alone is responsible for the success of Christian ministry (v. 7). For this reason, it is folly to boast in human ministers.

A clear allusion to the previous discussion of true wisdom (1:17; 2:9, 10 notes). The biblical concept of wisdom is broad enough to include artisans’ skills useful in construction (Ex. 31:2–6; 2 Chr. 2:13, 14), the metaphor for gospel ministry that Paul employs here.

**foundation.** As one called to proclaim the gospel where it was not known (v. 6 note), Paul had resolved to preach nothing but Christ crucified (v. 11; 2:2; cf. 1 Pet. 2:4–6).

These verses address the evaluation of Christian ministry. Some ministers who were seeking to build God’s building in Corinth, but who depended on human wisdom, were using perishable materials (“wood, hay, straw”) that would not survive the judgment of God’s fire, while the builders themselves would barely escape destruction. Without pressing Paul’s imagery too far, the perishable materials may be interpreted as either unsound teaching or the superficial and ephemeral “converts” that such teaching attracts for a time. Paul warns the church that they, like Solomon’s temple (1 Chr. 22:14–16), should be built up with what is lasting.

God signaled His presence in the temple by filling it with the cloud of His glory (1 Kin. 8:10, 11). Now He lives in His people by the Holy Spirit. Paul’s focus here is on God’s people as a corporate whole; in 6:19, the emphasis shifts to the individual Christian’s body.
Paul leaves open the possibility that some of the Christian builders in Corinth are not only using perishable material but are actively destroying God’s work. They will not be spared at the judgment.
Here the apostle returns more directly to the contrast between human and divine wisdom (v. 10 note), between the wisdom characteristic of this age—the flesh—and that of the age to come—the Spirit.

See note on 1:29.

**all things are yours.** This principle demonstrates the pettiness and absurdity of the Corinthians’ quarreling. If we belong to Christ, then because of Him all things belong to us (Rom. 8:17, 38, 39; Heb. 1:2), including each of the teachers around whom the cliques in Corinth gathered. Since every true gospel minister—whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas—is Christ’s gift to His whole church, rivalry and jealousy are needless and unfitting. How little the Corinthians appreciated their Christian privileges is pointed out again in 6:2. Paul will develop this point further in his treatment of spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 12–14).

Lest his reminder of the believers’ privilege tempt them to pride, Paul hastens to repeat that though he and Apollos are their servants (v. 5), their owner is Christ, who in turn belongs to God the Father, whose purpose and plan He came to accomplish (John 6:38).

These verses show that Paul was being judged and attacked by at least some of the Corinthians (2:1 note).

**stewards.** The steward was the preeminent servant in a Greco-Roman household, managing his master’s finances, property, and other slaves. Owning virtually nothing but controlling virtually everything, the steward wielded vast delegated authority, but always with accountability to the master to “be found faithful” (cf. Luke 12:42–48; 16:1–13, where the same Gk. word is rendered “manager”).

**mysteries.** See note on 2:7.

verse_quote: I do not even judge myself.
note: Though Paul’s conscience is clear (v. 5), ultimately only God determines whether one has proved faithful.

Not an absolute command (5:2; 6:2), but a warning not to usurp Christ’s role as judge in pronouncing final judgment. Paul speaks here to illegitimate criticisms raised against him.

**bring to light the things now hidden.** At the judgment, nothing will escape God’s searching light (Matt. 10:26 and parallels).

In this powerful passage, the apostle makes use of biting irony to show the Corinthians how trivial are their concerns and how unfair their criticisms. The sufferings of Paul are comparable to the pain and public humiliation of captives condemned to die (2 Cor. 11:23–30). In contrast, some of the Corinthians think of themselves as notably successful, but only because they do not understand what it means to be “fools for Christ’s sake” (v. 10)—not to behave nonsensically, but to identify with Christ’s cross, which seems foolish to the perishing but is God’s true wisdom (1:18–25). The deprivation, contempt, and manual labor experienced by the apostles disqualify and devalue their mission in the eyes of the world and of many in the church as well (2 Cor. 11:12—12:11).
Paul’s pastoral heart is revealed in these words. The harsh language of the previous passage was not intended to make them feel inferior but to raise their sensitivity to the truth.

The Corinthians boasted of their allegiance to Apollos, Peter, and others, with the implication that they had no need for Paul. The apostle reminds them that his fatherly relationship to them is unique and they have no good reason to attack him.
As the believers’ spiritual father, Paul consciously sets an example of selfless suffering to be followed by his children in Christ Jesus (11:1; Phil. 3:15–17).
Timothy had left prior to the writing of this letter (16:10 note). As Paul’s spiritual child, Timothy will show in his character and conduct what imitating Paul looks like (see Phil. 2:19–22).

verse_quote: as though I were not coming to you.
note: Some in Corinth argued that Paul was bold only when absent and that he was afraid to meet them face to face (2 Cor. 10:1, 2). He sent Timothy to them (v. 17), apparently to avoid an ugly confrontation, but he will not hesitate to come in person. It is up to them what will happen when that visit takes place (v. 21; 2 Cor. 13:1–10).

verse_quote: a man has his father’s wife.
note: The man’s father may have died, or the woman may have been a stepmother (more likely, since she is not called the man’s “mother”). In any case, the sexual relationship in view is the incestuous union explicitly condemned in Lev. 18:8. Though the Greco-Roman culture of Paul’s day tolerated a wide array of immoral activities, even Gentiles censured this kind of incest.

This verse is the key to Paul’s real concern. The underlying problem here was not the sin of one individual, but the failure of the Corinthian church to deal with the sin—indeed, their sense of pride in tolerating it (v. 6). Possibly, the Corinthians had developed a theology that could accommodate such immorality under the guise of celebrating their liberty in Christ from the restrictions of God’s law, articulated in their slogan, “all things are lawful for me” (6:12; 10:23). They needed to grasp their responsibility to exercise discipline and defend Christ’s reputation by excommunicating the offender (“removed from among you”).

A very difficult passage. Though Paul is physically absent from the Corinthian community, he claims to pass authoritative judgment in their midst. The apostle is commanding the church to expel the offender from their fellowship (“deliver this man to Satan”). The purpose of this judgment is the reclamation of the offender, but that can be achieved only if his sinful tendencies are overcome (“the destruction of the flesh”). According to one interpretation of 2 Cor. 2:5–11, this man did repent of his sin. See theological note “Excommunication” on p. 1703.

See notes on v. 2; 1:29.

**leaven.** Leaven is a common biblical metaphor for a corrupting influence (Matt. 16:11–12; Gal. 5:9). During the annual Feast of Passover, the Israelites removed all leaven from their houses (Ex. 12:15). So another purpose for church discipline, besides reclaiming the sinner (v. 5) and upholding Christ’s reputation for purity (v. 1; see 1 Pet. 2:11–12), is to protect other believers from being influenced toward evil by the offender’s example and the church’s condoning complacency.

Paul makes this important qualification to encourage the Corinthians; in a fundamental sense, they are already purified (1:2 note). He calls the Corinthians to embrace a lifestyle in keeping with their identity in Christ.

**Christ, our Passover.** The apostle develops the imagery by suggesting that the death of the Passover lamb instead of Israel’s firstborn (Ex. 12–13), as a shadow of better things to come (Heb. 10:1), pointed forward to the death of Christ.

verse_quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival.
note: The final, and especially beautiful, step in Paul’s argument is to draw a parallel between the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the life of purity that Christians should lead. This parallel helps us to understand the spiritual realities to which the OT ceremonies point (cf. Col. 2:16).

Prior to the writing of 1 Corinthians, Paul had sent a letter (no longer in existence) instructing the Corinthians to separate themselves from believers who practiced immorality. The Corinthians either misunderstood Paul, as if he were commanding complete separation from the world, or they tried to sidestep the issue by arguing that his request was unreasonable. The apostle explains that he had in mind anyone thought to be a Christian whose life openly contradicted the faith. The injunction to expel offenders (“not even to eat with such a one”) has primary reference to community life within the church and probably does not mean that all personal contact must be avoided ( “warn him as a brother”; 2 Thess. 3:15).

By quoting the frequent command in Deuteronomy (e.g., Deut. 17:7) to purge or expel the wicked from Israel, Paul draws an important parallel between the OT covenant community and the Christian church (10:1–11), while also implying a difference. Ancient Israel was to maintain its communal purity through banishment and execution, whereas in the new covenant the church’s disciplinary means are spiritual rather than physical. The church has authority to exercise discipline within its own fellowship, not to regulate the behavior of non-Christians. Paul assumes that believers can discern the boundary between those who are members of the church and under its spiritual supervision and those who are “outside” (Matt. 18:15–17)., 13

verse_quote: dare go to law before the unrighteous.
note: With this verse, Paul appears to change the topic from the evils of immorality to the problem of lawsuits among Christians. It is important, however, to notice the connection. In the first place, the topic of immorality has not been abandoned, but will recur in v. 9 and vv. 12–20. Second, the failings of the Corin­thians with regard to lawsuits are an expression of the problem already discussed in ch. 5, namely, a weak doctrine of the church. Just as Christians are not responsible to regulate the lives of non-Christians, so non-Christians have no power to discipline in the church. If the Corinthians understood the relation between the Israelite community and the Christian fellowship (5:12, 13 note), they would realize it was absurd for believers to go outside the church to solve their disputes. Who could imagine a pagan Gentile settling disputes among Israelites in the wilderness? This text does not, however, negate the legitimate role of civil authorities to judge matters that God has put under them. See theological note “Civil Government” on p. 2004.

The absurdity of the situation in Corinth becomes clearer when one recognizes that, in the consummation of history (but not before; 5:12, 13), Christians will participate with Christ in judging not only unbelievers but also wicked angels. Even the least qualified among the Corinthians, since he has received God’s Spirit and wisdom (2:14–16), is in a better position than an unbeliever to arbitrate disputes in the church.

This remarkable question makes obvious how critical is the principle of community for the apostle. The point is not that Christians should be encouraged to acquiesce passively to abuse from others. After all, cheating and injustice should not even exist within the Christian community. That such injustices do exist, and are indeed performed by Christians against one another, demonstrates how far the Corinthians have fallen. Nevertheless, if the Corinthians understood the serious implications of all the improprieties in their church, and if they appreciated the qualities that should characterize believers (cf. 13:4–7), they would much sooner bear injustice than bring disgrace upon the Christian community by publicly exposing their conflicts in the civil courts.

verse_quote: the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God.
note: See theological note “Antinomianism” on p. 2272. That the things of this world are incompatible with the kingdom of God is a recurring principle in Scripture (15:50; Gal. 5:21). The question arises whether anyone at all can be saved, since none is sinless. Paul’s answer is twofold: on the one hand, God delights in justifying the wicked (Rom. 4:5); on the other hand, those whom God justifies (declares righteous because of Christ’s death) He also sanctifies (leads into a holy way of life; Rom. 6:1–4). Paul charitably regards the Corinthians in terms of their profession as believers, justified and sanctified (v. 11 note), and therefore considers their present misbehavior as an anomaly that can be corrected. But it must be corrected. Persistence in wickedness would be an indication that their possession of faith is false and that they have no true place in the kingdom.

See notes on 1:2; 5:7; theological note “The Holy Spirit as Sanctifier” on p. 2023. The saving work of God’s Spirit through Jesus’ name includes not only legal vindication (“justified”) but also subjective purification and transformation (“sanctified”).

Paul may be quoting sayings, probably common in Corinth, that were used to excuse immoral behavior (note the repetition, again with qualifying corrections, at 10:23). The apostle’s corrective rejoinders suggest that, even if there is an element of truth in these slogans, the Corinthians have perverted it. Indeed, his qualifications have the effect of denying the very point of the sayings, and he ends by emphasizing the noble purpose for which God has given us bodies. Freedom in Christ is deployed in what is “helpful” to others, and does not lead us into being “dominated” by sinful desires, a senseless return to enslavement.

**Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food.** Another Corinthian slogan, this may assume a parallel between hunger for food and the sexual drive as a pretext for justifying any form of sexual indulgence as natural and irresistible. Paul will not permit such trivializing of sexuality, nor of the physical body itself. Its appointed end, for Christians, is not destruction in the grave but resurrection by God’s power to enjoy eternal blessing in the new heaven and earth (15:20–23, 35–58; Rev. 21:1–8). Those who die before the return of Christ and the final resurrection enjoy a spiritual existence with Christ in heaven (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:21–23), and their spirits will be reunited with their bodies at the resurrection., 13

This reference to the resurrection is unexpected here, and probably reflects the connection between inadequate doctrine and deficient life. Many of the Corinthians appear to have mistakenly denied the future bodily resurrection, believing that Christians have been fully been brought out of this age and fully brought into the age to come (ch. 15; 15:35 note). This was an erroneous understanding of eschatology (the last things), in which the only resurrection that is to take place is a spiritual resurrection, which had already occurred. But just as Christ was physically raised from the dead, so will all believers be physically raised at the very end of time. With such a false doctrine, some of the Corinthians may have regarded sexual relationships as unnecessary because sexual relations belong to this present age (7:1–5). The same doctrine could yield the opposite view: since what is done with the physical body has no spiritual significance, even promiscuous sexual behavior is not wrong.

verse_quote: your bodies are members of Christ.
note: The doctrine of the believer’s union with Christ is one of the most fundamental teachings of the apostle. What is significant about this verse is that it represents that union as involving the whole person, including the physical body (Rom. 12:1). The Corinthians were wrong in thinking that sexual union with a prostitute, just because it was physical, did not affect their relationship with Christ.

verse_quote: one body with her ... one spirit with him.
note: Paul assumes the truth of Gen. 2:24 (see Eph. 5:31), that sexual intercourse effects a profound interpersonal union that is more than merely physical. The contrast is not that union with Christ is spiritual while union with a prostitute is physical; Paul has emphasized in v. 15 that union with Christ involves the body, a point developed in vv. 18–20. “One spirit” probably refers to the Holy Spirit (15:45 note). Through the Holy Spirit we (spirit and body) have become one with Christ, and this sublime union forbids our giving our bodies to prostitutes. If what Paul condemns here has to do with the prostitutes who served at the temple of the goddess Aphrodite, the religious implications of the Corinthians’ immorality are even more obvious (10:20)., 17

The meaning of this passage is disputed. There seem to be many sins that are against the body. Nevertheless, in Paul’s teaching, the physical union involved in sexual immorality has special consequences because it interferes with our Christian identity as people who have been united with Christ through the Holy Spirit. It is perhaps significant that Paul’s prohibition in this verse (“Flee from sexual immorality”) is expressed in the same way as the command against idolatry (10:14).

verse_quote: a temple of the Holy Spirit.
note: Here Paul applies to the individual the concept of the church as the new temple where God dwells (3:16 note). While we must give due weight to this personal character of the Holy Spirit’s indwelling of individuals, the emphasis in Scripture is on the corporate identity of God’s people as a holy temple and a spiritual house (Eph. 2:19–22; 1 Pet. 2:4, 5).

verse_quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote.
note:
See Introduction: Date and Occasion.

**It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.** Very possibly this saying was used by an ascetic group among the Corinthian Christians who not only condemned sexual promiscuity (rightly) but also argued (wrongly) that Christians should avoid marriage and abstain from sexual relations even in marriage. The apostle had to be careful lest his teaching be distorted in one direction or another. Paul does not simply dismiss the slogan; he too opposes sexual immorality, and he recognizes a certain value in remaining unmarried (vv. 7, 8). He can give specific and valid reasons why a Christian may decide to stay single (vv. 29–35). But he must correct those who demand celibacy. In different contexts, Paul speaks of marriage in only positive terms (e.g., Eph. 5:22–33; 1 Tim. 3:2), and he condemns those who forbid marriage (1 Tim. 4:3).

These are remarkable verses in that they reveal viewpoints that appear to be far ahead of their time: a healthy perception of the woman’s sexuality, and an understanding of the complete equality that exists between a man and a woman in the most intimate area of their relationship. The Scripture gives no support whatever to the notion that sexual relations are solely at the direction and for the enjoyment of the husband. The apostle allows for temporary abstention from sex (in a way similar to fasting; v. 5), but he does not allow protracted abstinence. Sexual union is an expected part of marriage, not only a delight but also a debt owed to one’s wife or husband.

The “concession” probably refers to the brief periods of abstinence in v. 5: spouses may—but need not—deprive each other for a short period and for a specific reason. It may, however, refer to the marital state in general, which is not demanded of all believers but permitted to those with that calling. On the other hand, remaining unmarried has certain advantages for the work of the kingdom and the advance of the gospel, as Paul had been called to do. Nevertheless, the apostle realizes that a celibate life is not possible for everyone and that singleness would lead many Christians into sexual temptation.

In v. 12, Paul says, “I, not the Lord,” but Paul is not suggesting that there is an opposition between what he says and what the Lord says. With regard to the problem treated in vv. 10, 11, there was a well-known instruction given by Jesus during His earthly ministry (Mark 10:1–12). In vv. 12–16, however, Paul discusses a difficult situation that had not been expressly addressed by the Lord while He walked the earth. His apostolic commands, however, come by inspiration and have divine authority, as 14:37 makes clear (and is implied in Paul’s surprising understatement in 7:40).

In spite of the Lord’s command, it appears that some of the wives in Corinth, influenced by an ascetic viewpoint (v. 1), had in fact left their husbands. Because spouses are committed to each other until death (v. 39), even if they depart they may not remarry. Jesus had stated that a spouse’s sexual infidelity provides grounds that allow for (but do not require) divorce (Matt. 19:2–9); but Paul here deals with separation for other reasons that do not breach the marital covenant itself.

See note on v. 10. Jesus’ previous teaching on divorce presupposed that both husband and wife belonged to the covenant community. As the gospel invaded pagan cultures and communities, a new situation arose in which one spouse might come to trust Christ while the other would not (see 1 Pet. 3:1–7).

**who is an unbeliever.** This is the special circumstance about which Jesus had left no direct instructions. If one spouse has been converted and the other not, should the marriage therefore be dissolved, especially if the unbelieving spouse separates?

A striking affirmation of the special character of the home in which at least one parent is a believer (1:2 note). In OT language, the whole family is regarded as being in covenant with God. Even the spouse who refuses to believe comes under the influence of God’s work (v. 16)—much more so the children who are not old enough to profess their faith. Accordingly, Reformed theology has viewed this verse as providing part of the rationale for the baptism of the children of at least one professing believer. Because children of at least one believing parent are set apart, it is right to apply to these children the visible sign and seal of their separation from the world and incorporation into the covenant community. See notes on Acts 2:39; 16:15.

The thrust of this passage is that a Christian is not obligated to insist that the marriage remain intact. Such an insistence would prevent them from living in “peace.” If the unbelieving spouse deserts the marriage, the believing partner may accept or seek a divorce, and subsequently remarry.

Paul may be returning to the thought of v. 14 and giving a reason why Christians should not leave their unbelieving spouses: since they are in some sense “sanctified,” they are in a sphere within which they may be saved. Alternatively, v. 16 may explain v. 15: let the unbeliever go, because you have no assurance that he or she will be saved by being forced to stay married.

verse_quote: let each person lead the life ... God has called him.
note: The following verses make clear that the phrase “God has called him” speaks to the circumstances within which God places a believer in order to serve Him. Note that vv. 17–24 set forth a principle that gives coherence to the whole chapter: becoming a believer does not require a change in status, whether marital, ethnic, or social (vv. 8, 20, 26). This verse has sometimes been misused as evidence that Christians should not attempt to improve their social or economic standing. On the contrary, Paul encourages slaves to obtain their freedom if the opportunity arises (v. 21), while assuring believers that they can live to God’s glory and “with God” (v. 24) even when their living situations cannot be changed.

The first part of this verse is paralleled in Gal. 5:6 and 6:15. It would seem that the second part (“keeping the commandments of God”) is another way of saying, “faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6), and that faith that bears the fruit of love is what characterizes the “new creation” (Gal. 6:15).

The desire to attain a better condition is not wrong, as the rest of the verse makes clear. However, Paul does not want Christians troubling themselves about a situation that cannot be changed. Dissatisfaction and complaint can be fatal spiritually (10:10): they reflect lack of confidence in God.

This statement supports v. 22. Here and in its previous appearance (6:20) it reminds believers of Christ’s death and its inevitable result, that we are not our own but belong, body and soul, to the divine Redeemer who gave Himself for us. If we truly understood whose we are, we would realize that even slavery cannot damage our privileged position in Christ. Conversely, even the greatest human master is only a humble servant before Christ. Therefore, Christians need not, and must not, “become slaves of men.”

A new, but related topic that the Corinthians had raised in their letter to Paul (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**I have no command from the Lord.** See note on v. 10.

**I give my judgment.** This language suggests that the comments Paul are about to make are not absolute commandments for all circumstances, but recommendations for a particular situation. This interpretation is confirmed by the statement in v. 28 and by the concluding words in v. 38.

Lit. “the present necessity.” Some believe that Paul is referring to a specific and unusual problem in Corinth. However, the language of v. 28 (“will have worldly troubles”) suggests a more general idea: the predicament that faces all Christians as they seek to serve Christ in the present evil age (Gal. 1:4). We must consider this factor when making a decision about marriage, though other considerations should also be kept in mind (vv. 6–9 note).

verse_quote: the appointed time ... very short ... this world is passing away.
note: The Christian life must be lived in the realization that this present age will pass away at Christ’s return, when the age to come will be brought to consummation. Since Christians must always be ready for the coming of the Lord, there is no time to waste (Rom. 13:11, 12), as this age is already in process of “passing away.”

Despite first appearances, Paul is not exalting the single, celibate life as spiritually superior to the call to marriage, which necessarily entails anxiety “about worldly things” and pleasing one’s spouse. He offers realistic pastoral counsel, noting that those with the calling to singleness (which includes the gift of celibacy, v. 7) are spared the divided interests that require husbands and wives to attend to their spouses’ desires and needs. Elsewhere (notably Eph. 5:22–33), Paul stresses that a married person’s sacrificial and submissive love toward his or her spouse, far from competing with “undivided devotion to the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:35), beautifully expresses that devotion.

There are two different ways of understanding this passage. We simply do not know for certain whether Paul is addressing men who have deferred marriage to their fiancée (“betrothed”) or fathers who have not permitted their daughters to marry. However, the main idea is clear: both being married and being unmarried are good options, even though Paul sees a particular benefit in remaining unmarried.

Marriage is a lifelong commitment.

**free to be married.** A widow, no less than the others treated in this chapter, has the choice to remain unmarried or to marry. The only consideration is that if she marries again, the new spouse must be a Christian.

verse_quote: Now concerning food offered to idols.
note:
The Corinthians had raised the issue of idolatry dealt with in chs. 8–10, but the precise nature of their question is difficult to determine. According to some interpreters, the issues discussed in ch. 8 and in 10:25–30 are one and the same. Others, on the basis of 8:10, argue that ch. 8 deals with the serious problem that some Christians were attending pagan feasts and eating the food served there, while 10:25–30 concerns the lesser problem of meat purchased in the market and served in homes.

**all of us possess knowledge.** Paul addresses the sin of arrogance as an introduction to the subject of idolatry (vv. 1–3). These comments reveal that behind the behavior of the Corinthians (or at least an important group among them) lay a serious problem of attitude. Their conduct was not guided by love (cf. ch. 13) but by pride, an overconfidence in what they thought was a full and complete spiritual knowledge.

The Corinthians should be less concerned about what they know than about who knows them (cf. 13:12). God’s “knowing” people entails His personal, sovereign choice and love toward them (Gal. 4:9; Rom. 8:29; Amos 3:2), not merely acquaintance with information about them. Such sovereign grace should lead the Corinthians to the humility that they lack.

verse_quote: an idol has no real existence.
note: Apparently some of the Corinthians used the doctrine of monotheism as an argument supporting their practice: If there is only one God, who teaches us to mock idols (Is. 46:6, 7), why should we worry about eating food offered to them? Paul acknowledges this truth and affirms it (vv. 4–6), but goes on to point out an error in the Corinthians’ use of this doctrine.

Believers who have weak consciences are unable to dissociate various elements in pagan rituals from idolatry itself. When they eat food offered to idols, their consciences become “defiled.” Such strong language (cf. “destroyed” in v. 11) suggests that these weak Christians are sinning not merely because they think they are doing something wrong, but because they have fallen back into their idolatrous ways.
See note on v. 1 (cf. 10:18–22).

What was a source of pride for some of the Corinthians became the instrument that harmed others (v. 1 note).

**destroyed.** Paul underscores the seriousness of this matter—this professing believer may so fall from his profession of Christianity as to be “destroyed.”

Although the conscience is not infallible, it is a serious matter to violate it or tempt others to do so. Addressing similar dietary issues among the Christians at Rome, Paul taught that any action that does not proceed from faith—that violates one’s sense of what pleases God—is sin (Rom. 14:23).

This concluding comment is intended to set forth the basic principle of love: seeking the good of others above one’s own good (10:24, 33; 13:5; Phil. 2:4). Paul is about to discuss his willingness to forgo his legitimate rights and freedoms as an apostle to reinforce this point through his own example (9:1–23).

Paul’s willingness to forgo some of his rights is an illustration of the principle he states in 8:9. The questions in v. 1 may indicate that some in Corinth were questioning Paul’s authority and criticizing his behavior (v. 3). Or they simply highlight the noncontroversial evidence of his apostolic authority (as v. 2 affirms; cf. 2 Cor. 3:1–3) to show that he has demonstrated the mindset that he is requiring of the Corinthians, the readiness to forfeit personal rights for others’ well-being.

This statement makes explicit that Paul had indeed been criticized, though scholars debate the specific nature of the complaint (2:1 note). The next ten verses contain more than a dozen rhetorical questions that reflect Paul’s deep emotion and provide clues about the historical situation. Paul defends his right to be supported by the churches, only to emphasize his choice not to receive support (vv. 15–18). Perhaps some of the Corinthians were upset because Paul refused their patronage, and concluded from this that he was not a legitimate apostle (2 Cor. 11:7–12). If he is not, why should they listen to his instruction?

The Corinthians themselves may have raised this issue, as though the lack of a wife discredited Paul and Barnabas, or it may be Paul’s choice of an illustration to indicate the distinction between having a right and exercising it. Both Paul and Barnabas were unmarried at the time of their missionary work, but others labored as apostles while married. Paul takes for granted that if he were to be married, it would be with a believer, a “sister” in the Lord (see text note).

verse_quote: we have not made use of this right.
note: In spite of the strain that his secular work added to the heavy demands of his apostolic ministry, Paul was determined not to become a burden to the churches (1 Thess. 2:6–9) even though being supported by them was his “right” (9:8–14). It appears from 2 Cor. 11:7–12 that the Corinthians misinterpreted Paul’s motives. For reasons that are unclear, the apostle did make an exception in the case of the Philippian church in Macedonia (Phil. 4:15, 16). Perhaps he permitted established churches to be his financial partners while refusing “compensation” from those to whom he was first introducing the good news, freely offering God’s free grace, so that his ministry practice matched his message (v. 18).

verse_quote: get their living by the gospel.
note: This principle is reflected not only in the OT priesthood (v. 13) but also in several NT passages (e.g., Luke 10:7; Gal. 6:6; 1 Tim. 5:17, 18).

As the rest of the passage makes clear, Paul considers that he could hardly boast about preaching since he is compelled by God’s will to preach. So his ground for boasting (his “reward”) is that he preaches free of charge (v. 18), and he will not allow anyone to take this away from him., 16

Paul returns to the first question of v. 1. It appears that Paul must defend himself from the charge of inconsistency: he exercised freedom in his own behavior and therefore should not deprive others from doing the same. The apostle will return to this theme again in 10:23–33.

When ministering to Jews, Paul conforms to the OT ceremonial regulations even though he knows that these matters were not essential (Acts 16:1–3; 18:18; 21:20–26). See theological note “The Threefold Use of the Law” on p. 273.

When ministering to Gentiles, Paul is willing to live like them (for example, with respect to the Mosaic dietary laws), while recognizing that he is never free to disobey God’s moral law, or the “law of Christ.”

A restatement of the point made in 8:13.

**all things to all people.** This generalization and that in 10:33 (“I try to please everyone in everything”) must be read in light of the apostle’s insistence that he seeks always to be within God’s law and under Christ’s law (v. 21 note). In any matter that was morally indifferent from the standpoint of God’s revealed will, Paul will gladly set aside his personal preferences to further the gospel’s reception by others and the gospel’s work in them.

verse_quote: run that you may obtain it.
note: Paul elsewhere uses the illustration of a race and its prize to emphasize the need for single-mindedness, determination, and perseverance (Phil. 3:12–14; 2 Tim. 4:7, 8).

He continues the athletic metaphor by reminding his readers that fighters must discipline their bodies if they expect to win. Similarly, Christians must be willing to set aside their selfish interests for the sake of their primary goal (cf. 1 Tim. 4:7–8; 2 Tim. 2:5).

**lest ... I myself should be disqualified.** This statement has often been used as evidence that Christians can lose their salvation. The witness of the NT and of Paul in particular is that those whom God has brought to Himself are His forever (Rom. 8:28–30) because the life they have been given in Christ is eternal in character (John 5:24; cf. Heb. 7:16). What God has begun He will bring to completion (Phil. 1:6). However, it would be wrong to dismiss or minimize Paul’s concern (cf. 15:2; Phil. 3:11; Col. 1:23) by suggesting that it is merely hypothetical or relates only to rewards and not salvation. Paul was confident that absolutely nothing would be able to separate him from God’s love (Rom. 8:38–39), but he never presumed that he was saved regardless of what he did. No Christian can afford to take lightly the warnings of Scripture (10:12), because these warnings are the God-appointed means by which true believers persevere to the end. Those of faith heed these warnings, as the Spirit works through them to make them will and work “for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13).

Christian baptism signifies the union of the believer with Christ, and Paul uses the language of baptism in comparing the Israelites and the Corinthians (5:12, 13 note). All the Israelites went through the ordeal and deliverance of the exodus by virtue of their identification with their leader, Moses. Note the repetition of “all” in vv. 1–3 (also 12:13). “All” the members of the Corinthian church have been baptized into Christ, and in that respect have been identified with God’s deliverance in Christ, but baptism does not guarantee that God is pleased with each baptized individual without exception. This passage illustrates and explains the warning in 9:24–27. Heb. 3:7–4:13 (especially 3:16–4:2) draws the same cautionary lesson from the privileges and the judgment experienced by Israel’s wilderness generation. Apart from saving faith, the external rite of baptism accomplishes nothing.

verse_quote: the same spiritual food ... the same spiritual drink.
note:
Following the analogy with baptism, Paul warns the Corinthians not to find false comfort in their participation in the Lord’s Supper (vv. 14–22). The Israelites also experienced divinely given food and drink. Here “spiritual” does not mean “immaterial,” but that it was supplied miraculously by God’s power. Paul probably has in mind the activity of the Holy Spirit (2:6, 14; 3:1; 15:44–46; and notes). The Israelites had received a supernatural provision associated with the work of the Spirit.

**the Rock was Christ.** In the OT, God is often compared with a rock, and Israel (called “Jeshurun”) is described as having forsaken God, the “Rock of his salvation” (Deut. 32:15). The Lord identified Himself in a special way with the rock that gave forth water at Massah and Meribah, for He stood “before” Moses on the rock as it was struck (Ex. 17:5–6). The analogy between the Israelites and the Corinthians is not an arbitrary illustration; there is a theological connection, so Paul identifies the rock as a “type” of Christ (vv. 6, 11 notes). Without minimizing the privileges enjoyed by Christians (v. 11 note), Paul reminds us that the Deliverer of the Israelites was none other than our crucified and risen Savior., 4

These verses narrate Israel’s sin of idol worship in the wilderness, after the Israelites left Egypt. The clearest OT reference to Israel’s sin of idolatry in 10:5–11 is a quotation from Ex. 32:6 in v. 7: “And do not be idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written, ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and stood up to play.’” This was a description of the Israelites in their raucous worship of the calf idol. This quotation forms a central part of vv. 5–11, which is then the basis for the exhortations in vv. 12–14.

The Gk. word (_typos_) is related to the English term “type” (so also in v. 11). The use of this word likely further indicates that the events of the wilderness have a divinely intended correspondence with the experiences of the Christian church. Israel, in the wilderness of her pilgrimage, serves as a formative example for the church in her pilgrimage, now that redemptive history has reached fulfillment in the coming of Christ (v. 11 note).

verse_quote: the end of the ages has come.
note: This statement reflects Paul’s conviction that the coming of Christ inaugurated the “last days” (Heb. 1:2), the time when the great promises of the OT come to pass (cf. 1:20 note). By pointing out this theme, Paul helps the Corinthians to realize that the OT events narrated here about Israel’s idolatry in vv. 5–11 looked forward and applied to them. Israel’s idolatry foreshadowed the idolatry of some in Corinth and stands also as a warning to what will happen to those in Corinth who commit idolatry (see 10:14, 20–22) as Israel did (note in this respect vv. 12, 14). Moreover, these facts suggest that given their privileged position, the Corinthians ought to recognize their greater responsibility (cf. Heb. 11:39, 40).
See note on 9:27. Receiving the benefits described in 10:1–4 did not inoculate idolatrous Israelites against God’s judgment (10:5–11). The same principle applies in the church today.

This well-known verse has provided great encouragement to Christians facing temptations. At the same time, Paul’s words contain an implicit rebuke. If God keeps us from temptations greater than we can withstand, we cannot plead our temptations as an excuse for sinning. Sin is never a necessity for a believer.

**the way of escape ... you may be able to endure it.** Paul’s carefully chosen words imply that at times “escape” from temptation will not entail a change of circumstances, but the Holy Spirit’s power to withstand and endure (2 Cor. 12:2–10).

This command is related to Paul’s previous remarks about eating food offered to idols (8:1 note; 8:10). Specifically, Paul is grieved that some of the Corinthians were participating in pagan meals that had an inseparable element of idolatry (see Rev. 2:14, 20).

verse_quote: The cup of blessing ... The bread that we break.
note: These statements about the Lord’s Supper demonstrate the significance of taking part in a distinctively religious meal. Just as it would be impossible to take the Lord’s Supper and claim that it had no religious significance, so it is naive for the Corinthians to think they can participate in temple feasts without being involved in idolatry. Another point is that the unity “in the body of Christ” symbolized by taking the bread and wine excludes union with idols. See theological note “The Sacraments” on p. 1726.

. Later Paul will show the implications of the unity of the church in the body of Christ, symbolized by the bread, both for believers’ relationships as they observe the Supper (11:23–34) and for their exercise of spiritual gifts to build each other up in unity (12:12–31).
Although idols are nothing (v. 19), behind pagan rituals is the reality of Satan’s work, and Christians should have nothing to do with that.

See note 6:12, 13. Again the apostle qualifies and corrects the Corinthians’ slogan of liberty, calling them to use their freedom to help and build up others, seeking “the good of his neighbor” (v. 24), rather than for self-indulgence.

verse_quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market.
note: In spite of his strong words against taking part in idolatrous feasts, Paul does not want the Corinthians to be overly scrupulous. The fact that food is offered to an idol does not change what the food is; it is still part of God’s creation, as the citation from Ps. 24:1 (v. 26) shows. Therefore, the Corinthian believers do not have to ask whether food in the market was brought from the temple, nor do they need to raise the question when invited to a meal (v. 27). They may freely eat what God has provided.

A different problem arises if someone announces that the meat comes from a pagan sacrifice. Presumably, such a comment indicates that the speaker is a Christian who has problems of conscience about it, or even a pagan (“offered in sacrifice” reflects a Gk. term, “sacrificed to a holy thing,” which differs from the term “offered to idols” elsewhere in this passage [8:1, 4, 7, 10; 10:19; see Acts 15:29; Rev. 2:14, 20]). In that case, it is right to abstain “for the sake of the one who informed you,” lest he mistake your consumption for worship of an idol.

To voluntarily refrain from a practice that Christ’s law permits for the sake of avoiding misperception by one who is weaker in faith (8:7) is not to forfeit one’s true freedom of conscience in Christ.
This question suggests that Paul had been accused of eating meat offered to idols, with the suggestion that he has no right to forbid the Corinthians to do the same (9:19 note).

verse_quote: do all to the glory of God.
note: Paul brings his argument in chs. 8–10 to its climax—the Christian’s every decision is to be governed and determined by what will promote the manifested excellence of God through the drawing of Jews and Greeks to faith and the strengthening of the church of God (v. 32).

verse_quote: please everyone in everything I do.
note:
See note on 9:22. When the purity of the gospel was at stake, Paul had no interest at all in pleasing people (Gal. 1:8–10). But where his personal preferences were concerned, he gladly subjected them to God’s greater purpose, the salvation of His elect from all nations.

**not seeking my own advantage, but that of many.** In conjunction with the desire to do everything for God’s glory (v. 31), this principle provided Paul with his criterion of behavior. The submission of one’s own advantage to what will promote the salvation of others is the principle of Christian love, which “does not insist on its own way” (13:5).
The apostle does not set himself up as an absolute example; he is to be imitated to the extent that he imitates Christ.

Paul transitions to address a new cluster of topics pertaining to the church’s worship (vv. 2–34). He opens with a commendation for the Corinthians’ fidelity to apostolic tradition entrusted to them by Paul. One such tradition is the wording in which Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper (v. 23). He finds it necessary, however, to mingle commendation with correction both with respect to women’s roles in worship and with respect to the Corinthians’ observance of the Supper (see v. 17).

The significance of this metaphor has long been debated by scholars—it may indicate leadership and authority, or source and origin. The two ideas should probably not be regarded as excluding each other. In two other contexts where Paul speaks of Christ as head (Eph. 4:15; Col. 2:19), the notion of “source” may be present (cf. v. 8). Elsewhere, Paul uses the metaphor with explicit reference to authority or submission (Eph. 1:22; 5:23, 24; Col. 1:18; 2:10). Here the stress probably falls on authority rather than source (cf. v. 10).

The evidence of Greco-Roman statuary seems to indicate that Roman men typically pulled their togas over their heads when offering pagan sacrifices, whereas in the first-century Jewish men left their heads uncovered while worshiping. The Jewish custom of men covering their heads at prayer probably does not go back to the NT period.

**dishonors his head.** Probably a reference to Christ as the head (v. 7). Neither the Bible nor other documents explain why such a practice would dishonor Christ (cf. v. 10 note). Perhaps Paul’s point is that the Roman practice tended to obscure the visible distinction between men and women and thus blurred the complementary relationships of leadership and submission that, ultimately, reflect the submission to God the Father that Christ displays in His redemptive mission (v. 3).

Given the contrast with the previous verse, this comment suggests that Jewish women in the first century normally worshiped with a head covering. Some scholars think that Paul refers to a particular hairstyle (in Num. 5:18, loosening a woman’s hair is part of the test for an unfaithful wife).

**the same as if her head were shaven.** In v. 6, shaving a woman’s head is compared to having the hair cut short, presumably like a man’s. But this would “shame” the very man she is called to honor or glorify (v. 7). It appears then that Paul is opposing a practice that tended to obliterate the visual distinction between the sexes. Possibly, the controversy reflects the idea of some Corinthians that they had achieved spiritual perfection and were no longer subject to normal rules (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

verse_quote: woman is the glory of man.
note: See theological note “Human Beings Created in the Image of God” on p. 13. Paul is not saying that woman is man’s inferior (vv. 11–12), nor denying that God has made women after His image (Gen. 1:27). Rather, Paul stresses that each wife uniquely expresses the excellence of her husband.

Without devaluing woman’s and man’s equality as God’s image-bearers (v. 7 note), Paul sees in the order of their creation (Gen. 2:7, 22) a sign of the man’s functional leadership vis-à-vis the woman (1 Tim. 2:11–14). A counterbalancing reality, that henceforth every man is born of woman (vv. 11, 12), demands humility and an appreciation of our profound interdependence.

Many interpretations of this phrase have been suggested, but they are all speculative. Paul may be saying that it is particularly inappropriate to rebel against God’s created order in the presence of these glorious, holy creatures.

These verses appear to be a qualification of the previous comments, offering a balancing perspective that furthers our humility and unity. Not only are men in general dependent on women, their mothers, for biological birth, but also with specific reference to our relationship “in the Lord,” men and women are mutually dependent, since we are one in Him (Gal. 3:28)., 12

Interpreters differ about the meaning of this term. Some believe it refers to the created order. Others argue that the apostle is here appealing to the common practices of his day. The fact that Paul has already referred to the created order (v. 8) seems to make it more likely that Paul is referring to the created order.
Some argue that the hair is “in place of” a covering. But Paul may mean that since the woman’s long hair serves as a covering, it is equally appropriate for her to wear a veil.

Paul does not use exactly this kind of argument elsewhere in any of his letters. Such a conclusion to a difficult passage may give some support to the view that the apostle was not prescribing permanent forms of worship. However, the apostle’s appeal to the created order (vv. 8, 14) must be taken into account as suggesting that Paul’s instruction transcends the specific circumstances of the Corinthian church. In any case, even if Paul is dealing with questions of cultural appropriateness, such questions have theological implications (v. 5 note). Without a doubt, there is an underlying theological principle to Paul’s teaching on head coverings that remains constant in every age—the concreated roles and relationships between husband and wife. The husband is to lead his wife in godliness, and his wife is to submit to his leadership as he does so (cf. Eph. 5:22–33).
The contrast between these words and v. 2 indicates the seriousness of the problem that Paul now addresses, which concerns abuses of the Lord’s Supper.

verse_quote: there must be factions among you.
note: Paul recognizes that nothing occurs outside the divine will and that God may use human sin to further His own purposes. Or, more probably, Paul may be using irony, trying to make the Corinthians see that their infighting has the unworthy motive of seeing who can argue the best.
Their mishandling of this observance has turned it into something quite different from what it should be.

verse_quote: One goes hungry, another gets drunk.
note: Paul’s concern here is not only with drunkenness but also with the humiliation of the poor. The Lord’s Supper symbolizes, among other things, the unity of God’s people (10:17). Those Corinthians who were well-off apparently did not share with the less fortunate among them at the feasts where the Lord’s Supper was celebrated. This selfish behavior openly contradicted the meaning of the ceremony.

Paul’s account of the institution of the Lord’s Supper is in all essentials the same as what the Gospels record, and the words of institution correspond most closely with those preserved in Luke (cf. Matt. 26:26–29; Mark 14:22–25; Luke 22:17–20). These verses clarify what it means to partake of the elements of the Supper in a worthy manner (v. 27) and with discernment (v. 29). They therefore guide the believer in the kind of self-examination that should properly precede his participation in the sacrament (v. 28). See theological note “The Lord’s Supper.”

verse_quote: you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
note: Note the connection between preaching the gospel and celebrating the Lord’s Supper. The Supper sets forth God’s Word through visible rather than verbal means. Note also that celebrating the Supper gives expression to our sure hope of the Lord’s return.

It is important to take this whole section together as a unit, and vv. 33, 34 make plain that Paul still has in mind the abuses mentioned in vv. 21, 22. Phrases such as “in an unworthy manner” (v. 27) and “Let a person examine himself” (v. 28) can be extended and applied to many circumstances, but we should be careful not to wrench them from their context. In particular, it would be a misreading of v. 30 to think that God routinely brings illness and death to Christians who, in spite of their spiritual failings, partake of the Supper. Because some of the believers in Corinth were celebrating the Supper in a way that both profaned the spiritual significance of the atoning death of Christ, of which the elements are sign and seal, and destroyed the unity the Supper represents, God had brought judgment upon the community. God’s purpose in judging these believers, however, was to prevent them from being “condemned along with the world” (v. 32).

This may refer to a failure to recognize that the bread of the Supper signifies Christ’s sacrificed body (vv. 24, 27) and, implicitly, this would include a failure to see the cup as a sign and seal of Christ’s shed blood. The fact that only the failure to “discern the body” is mentioned leads some scholars, however, to see the sin indicted here as conduct that disrupts the unity of the church as Christ’s body (10:17; 12:12 note) by indifferent neglect of the hungry poor in the congregation (v. 21).

As an introduction to the subject of spiritual gifts in Corinth, Paul reminds his readers of the contrast between their pagan and Christian experience. It is not clear whether anyone was actually uttering curses against Jesus (the statement may be only an illustration), but the focus of v. 3 is on the content of religious speech. Paul invokes the ancient and widespread criterion for evaluating new prophetic utterances, namely, their consistency with previous divine revelation (Deut. 13:1–5; 1 John 4:1–3). In view of 14:6–19, we may infer that the apostle is anticipating his argument for understandable speech. Pagans may likewise have experienced miraculous speech, but what really matters is what is said., 3

verse_quote: varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit.
note: Apparently, the Corinthians exaggerated the importance of the gift of tongues, so Paul must remind them that one and the same Spirit distributes a variety of gifts to His people. The added references to “the same Lord” (v. 5) and “the same God” (v. 6) reflect the importance of the doctrine of the Trinity for Paul; they also support his concern for unity within diversity.

We completely misunderstand the purpose of the Spirit’s gifts (here called a “manifestation”) if we use them for selfish reasons. Because there are different needs in the Christian community, different gifts are required. Furthermore, the Spirit gives gifts not for one’s personal aggrandizement, but for the edification of the body of Christ.

This list of gifts is not intended as a complete catalog (others are included in v. 28); possibly, it reflects gifts that were especially evident in Corinth. We need not assume that all of the gifts were manifested in every church. The list in Rom. 12:6–8, for example, includes only two of the gifts mentioned here (prophesying and faith) and omits those that might be thought of as miraculous, such as healing and tongues. In determining the character of some of the gifts listed here, we are hindered by the absence of descriptions of them anywhere in the NT. “The utterance of wisdom” may have been an ability to resolve difficult spiritual problems and “the utterance of knowledge” a special revelation of some sort, but we cannot be certain. Similarly, it is not clear why Paul lists separately the gifts of “faith,” “healing,” and “working of miracles.” The reference to “the ability to distinguish between spirits” perhaps should be understood in the light of 1 John 4:1–3. Our inability to determine the precise function of some of these gifts is not an obstacle to understanding the thrust of this passage, which aims not at giving detailed instruction about them but rather at emphasizing the variety of God’s endowments to His church (v. 11).

Although the word translated “tongue” is the normal Gk. word for “language” (_glossa_), the proper description of this gift has generated much debate. According to one view, it refers to some kind of ecstatic speech, possibly related to “the tongues ... of angels” mentioned in 13:1. According to another view, it refers to foreign languages. There is no reason to conclude that the “tongues” of 1 Corinthians differ from the “tongues” of Acts 2. The phenomenon of “tongues” described in Acts 2 was clearly foreign languages (Acts 2:6), and here Paul uses the same Gk. wordto describe this gift.

This brief clause sets the preceding list of gifts in the proper perspective. Whether an individual or a church possesses a particular gift is not for us to decide. It is the Spirit who sovereignly provides for the people of God. That factor may explain why no NT passage gives a complete catalog of gifts or a precise definition of them, since they may vary significantly according to God’s plans in changing situations. A church may appropriately pray for God to grant gifts to meet its needs, but such prayers must be offered in submission to His sovereign will and perfect wisdom.

See theological note “The Church” on p. 2094. The description of Christ’s church as a body is one of the most distinctive and significant teachings of Paul (1:13 note). Indeed, the apostle explains that he was given a special revelation concerning this “mystery,” which was hidden for many ages; namely, that God’s people, both Jews and Gentiles, are now constituted as one body, on equal terms, by virtue of Christ’s exaltation (Eph. 1:22, 23; 3:2–6). Both the existence and the growth of the church presuppose this unity established by Christ through the Spirit (Eph. 4:3–6, 11–16; Col. 2:19; 3:14, 15).

The emphasis on the word “all” and the allusion to the sacraments recalls the similar description of the Israelites in 10:2–4 (cf. notes). One of the truths signified and sealed by water baptism is the baptism of the Holy Spirit that incorporates believers into the one body of Christ. Baptism replaces circumcision as the sign of admission into God’s covenant (Col. 2:11–14). Similarly, partaking of the Lord’s Supper signifies our continued communion with Christ and His church (10:17; 11:29 note).

Having established the unity of Christ’s church, Paul sets forth its diversity. Some scholars have commented that the Corinthians’ most fundamental problem was not their rejection of the church’s unity, but rather their failure to acknowledge its diversity. Paul corrects this error through a comparison with the human body. He appeals to the sovereign will of God, who has “arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose” (v. 18; cf. v. 11). If the Corinthians denied the validity of certain gifts, they were really questioning God’s authority to distribute the gifts. Paul stresses unity, but not a uniformity that squelches valid forms of diversity in believers’ service to others.

This comparison manifests the problem that has occupied Paul throughout most of the letter, namely, a sense of spiritual superiority among some of the Corinthians and their consequent disdain for those who appear to be “weaker” and “less honorable.” Their devaluing of certain gifts (possibly in favor of the gift of tongues) is Paul’s concern here., 23

The items in this verse are different from those in vv. 8–10, providing that Paul is not interested in giving a complete list of spiritual gifts and offices. Here Paul begins with “apostles” and “prophets,” whom he considers the foundation (Eph. 2:20), and adds as a third category “teachers,” so that this listing is similar to that in Eph. 4:11. Though the Gk. words for “helping” and “administrating” do not occur elsewhere in the NT, Paul probably has in mind the gifts of one who “does acts of mercy” and the one who “leads,” respectively (Rom. 12:8).

These rhetorical questions bring to a climax Paul’s argument that we should not expect everyone to have the same gifts, since God apportions them as He wills (vv. 11, 18). See theological note “The Apostles” on p. 1912., 30

The meaning of this sentence is disputed. Some believe it refers to the more important gifts in v. 28 (especially prophecy, 14:1); others argue that it introduces the discussion of love in ch. 13. Most likely, Paul is anticipating what he will say later about gifts for “building up the church” (14:12), i.e., speaking “words with my mind in order to instruct others” (14:19).

**more excellent way.** Before explaining what the “higher gifts” are, as he will in ch. 14, Paul must point out what is the essential condition for the proper exercise of any gift—love.

Using intentional exaggeration, Paul emphasizes the uselessness of gifts exercised without love. The expression “tongues of men” probably refers to the gift of speaking in foreign languages (Acts 2:4–11), while the addition “and of angels” may be a deliberate exaggeration (similarly with “understand all mysteries” and “remove mountains”). Whether the Corinthians claimed to use angelic speech is impossible to determine (12:10 note). The expression “deliver up my body to be burned” may also be a dramatic overstatement.

Paul personifies love as a person who acts in the ways Christians should imitate. The total picture suggests a description of Christ Himself. Considering the kinds of problems this epistle addresses, these verses are a rebuke to the Corinthians, who were failing to conduct themselves with love (boastful and arrogant, 8:1; 12:21; insisting on one’s own way, 6:1–8; etc.).
Paul may mean that those who love do not devise evil against others. More likely, he means that those who love do not focus their attention on the wrongs that others do to them.
Paul uses this word four times for rhetorical effect as he brings his description of love to a climax.
