One could view this statement as a summary of the previous verse, especially in the light of the comment that love “bears all things.” At the same time, the statement allows Paul to build a contrast between love, which always remains (v. 13), and the spiritual gifts, which will cease when their purpose, to promote the growth of the church, is completed (Eph. 4:11–13).

**prophecies ... tongues ... knowledge.** It is likely that Paul mentions these three items because they were the spiritual gifts, of which the Corinthians were most proud. Some believe that these three gifts have a temporary, earthly function until the end of the age and will not continue at the consummation of the age to come. Others suggest that Paul mentions these three in particular because they have a revelatory function that came to an end with the completion of the NT canon (v. 10 note). This latter view is supported by Eph. 2:19, 20, where “apostles and [NT] prophets” are part of the “foundation” of the church temple, along with Christ as the “cornerstone.” Thus, like Christ, the revelatory function of the apostles and prophets, who gave us our NT canon, was a foundation-laying activity like Christ’s ministry, death, and resurrection. Thus, as with Christ, when the foundation-laying activity is accomplished, the activity is so unique that it ceases.

The context (especially v. 12) suggests strongly that Paul is here referring to the second coming of Christ as the final event in God’s plan of redemption and revelation. In comparison with what we will receive then, the present blessings are only partial and thus imperfect. It is therefore a sign of immaturity for the Corinthians to treat the temporary, incomplete gifts of the Spirit as having ultimate significance. According to another view, Paul may be referring to the “complete” revelation of the NT Scriptures, revelation that makes prophecy and other revelatory gifts obsolete.

verse_quote: I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
note: Perhaps because the Corinthians liked to boast of their knowledge (8:1 note), Paul concludes by stressing the partial character of all present knowledge. The shift from the active (“know”) to the passive (“have been known”) is found elsewhere in the apostle’s letters and serves to emphasize dependence on God’s grace (8:3; Gal. 4:9). Here the focus is on the intimacy and accuracy of God’s knowing, which we will share someday (though the infinity of His knowledge—His omniscience—will always set Him apart from even His glorified creatures).
See theological note “Love.”

Having set the discussion within the proper framework of love, Paul now encourages the Corinthians to recognize the value of the spiritual gifts. Because the Corinthians have exaggerated the importance of the gift of tongues, however, the emphasis of ch. 14 is on the understandable gifts (v. 19)—primarily prophecy, but also the interpretation of tongues (vv. 27, 28), which are the functional equivalent of prophecy. The superiority of prophecy to tongues lies in its power to communicate with hearers without the need of “interpretation,” thus furthering “their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation” (v. 3).

verse_quote: speaks not to men but to God ... utters mysteries.
note:
This verse (cf. v. 14) describes the gift of tongues in a way that seems inconsistent with the gift of speaking in foreign languages mentioned in Acts 2:4–11 (although some believe that the miracle on Pentecost was a miracle of hearing). Accordingly, many argue that Paul is dealing with something different—a kind of ecstatic speech used for intimate prayer (Rom. 8:26). However, the word translated “tongue” is the normal Gk. term for “language.” Second, Paul uses the term “mysteries” to indicate a divine truth not yet disclosed. The word does not have the meaning of the English word “mysterious” (2:7 note). Third, vv. 10, 11, as well as v. 21, support the idea that even here Paul is speaking of human languages (12:8–10 note).

**in the Spirit.** The “tongues” in view here are revelatory. What is spoken are matters divinely revealed by the Holy Spirit. As Peter’s quotation from Joel 2 implied, the “tongues” in which God’s mighty deeds were declared at Pentecost were a subcategory of prophecy, similar to God’s uttering His word through Joel and other OT prophets (Acts 2:16–18).

verse_quote: builds up himself ... builds up the church.
note: Those speaking in an uninterpreted language are encouraged and comforted. Unless the meaning of the message spoken in a “tongue” can be conveyed to others, however, the Holy Spirit’s purpose for His gifts—to build up the church—is not achieved (vv. 5, 12). Prophecy delivered in a language known to the speaker and the hearers is superior to tongues, needing no interpretation to accomplish its aim, the edification of others., 5
This principle of benefiting others by edifying them becomes the central point of the passage. Paul is applying the teaching of 12:7 that God has granted a variety of gifts “for the common good.”
These verses illustrate the principle mentioned in v. 6. Musical instruments convey nothing to those who listen unless they are played with intelligent purpose., 8

Without minimizing the significance of the gift of tongues, Paul encourages the Corinthians to use it in a way that makes it valuable for the congregation. At Pentecost, listeners who spoke various languages recognized their native dialects in the believers’ proclamation (Acts 2:8–11), but the Holy Spirit also bestowed on some Christians a supernatural gift to be able to interpret messages delivered in unknown languages (12:10, 28–30).

verse_quote: my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.
note: Whatever spiritual benefit he might receive from the experience, the exercise of this gift does not bear “fruit,” i.e., others are not built up. In the next verse, Paul emphasizes that he would rather have both benefits. Throughout this discussion, “my spirit” or “the spirits of the prophets” (vv. 14, 15, 16, 32) probably refers not to an aspect of the human personality distinguishable from one’s mind, but rather to “my manifestation of the (Holy) Spirit” (so v. 12), or simply, “my spiritual gift.”

The members of the congregation, if they are to participate in public worship, must be able to agree with the message of the hymns being sung and the prayers being offered. The custom of expressing their approval with an audible “Amen” (“So it is!”) cannot be followed if no one understands what has been said.

It may be that some of the Corinthians justified their emphasis on the gift of tongues by arguing that Paul himself exercised this gift. Without denying the fact, the apostle puts the gift in proper perspective by pointing out how much more valuable it is to do something “in order to instruct others.”, 19

Up to this point, Paul has been discussing the use of tongues among believers. But what about unbelievers who hear the tongues? In their concern for tongues, the Corinthians have ignored unbelievers, and Paul admonishes the church for this display of spiritual immaturity. He appeals to “the Law,” (the OT) to show that God uses unintelligible speech as a sign of His judgment. Is. 28:11 explains how God judged the Israelites through the Assyrians’ speaking a foreign language. If non-Christians come to public worship and hear an unintelligible language, they will be repelled (v. 23) and reject the gospel. In this situation, uninterpreted tongues are a sign of judgment “for unbelievers” (v. 22). But the Corinthians should aim at bringing unbelievers to repentance and to the recognition that God is present (v. 25). Because God uses the understandable words of prophecy to accomplish this purpose, prophecy is a sign “for believers”; it is evidence of God’s goodness to them (v. 22).

verse_quote: say that you are out of your minds.
note: Rather than being attracted, unbelievers will find unintelligible speech offensive and dismiss a message that makes no sense to them, as Palestinian Jews in the crowd at Pentecost accused the believers of drunkenness, while those from other nations recognized that the Christians were speaking their languages and understood the Christians’ message (Acts 2:12–13).

verse_quote: falling on his face ... God is really among you.
note: Paul alludes to the prophetic promise that foreigners will come, bow down, and acknowledge the Lord’s presence in Israel’s midst (Is. 45:14). This is one more indication that the church is now the true congregation of Israel that reveals God’s truth to Gentile unbelievers (note the use of “church” [_ekklēsia_] in v. 23, a word that in the Septuagint often refers to the congregation of Israel).
See note on v. 6.

This concern for understanding has informed the whole discussion (v. 1 note). Paul’s instructions in this verse and the following demonstrate that those who spoke in tongues controlled their utterance, although others may not have understood it.

Having given instructions for the proper exercise of the gift of tongues, Paul moves on to other directives that also affect the order of public worship. Since he had emphasized the importance of prophecy, he points out that even this gift should be exercised in an orderly fashion—“Let two or three prophets speak” (during the course of, or perhaps at various points in, the service)—while “the others” should explicate the message for the congregation. Apparently the Corinthians were speaking in tongues and prophesying without regard for each other or for the content of the message (12:2, 3 note). Their disorder was a threat to the unity of the body and was incompatible with the God “of peace” (v. 33).

These verses have created debate among Christians, at least partly because it is not known what problem exactly Paul was seeking to correct. It has even been proposed that these verses were not part of Paul’s original letter. In view of 11:5 and other NT passages, it is certain that Paul is not absolutely forbidding women to speak in every church situation. Paul may have been addressing a particular problem in Corinth, such as women creating disorder during the worship service. He likely has in mind a specific function, such as the evaluation of prophecy (vv. 29, 32), in which women should not participate because this is the role of church elders in their function of the doctrinal guardianship of the church (on which cf. 1 Tim. 2:11–14). Another view, supported by Paul’s direction that women should satisfy their “desire to learn” by asking their husbands at home, is that the Corinthian women were disruptively interrupting prophets or other teachers with their questions. This command is also related to Paul’s later prohibition against women teaching at 1 Tim. 2:12, although the latter concerns the official teaching authority exercised by overseers (elders; cf. 1 Tim. 3:1–7), though that passage might also concern the relationship of husbands to wives. Wives are to “subject themselves as the Law also says.” The “Law” here refers most likely to the OT, since all of Paul’s other uses of “Law” in 1 Corinthians have this meaning (see 1 Cor. 9:8, 9; 20 21; 14:21; 15:56); thus it does not refer to a law of nature or some kind of Greco-Roman law. Though there is debate about what particular text from the “Law” is in mind, the submissive behavior of women under the old covenant in Israel continues to be the same under the new covenant in the eschatological Israel, i.e., “in the churches.” Most likely, the particular reference is to Genesis 1–2, where the order of creation shows that Adam is the firstborn son of God (cf. Gen. 5:1–3) and high priest, which carries along with it authority over all creation, including authority over Eve. This is just what Paul argues in 1 Tim. 2:11–14 (cf. note). This is consistent with the emphasis on maintaining order “in all the churches of the saints” (v. 33)., 35

These sarcastic questions show that Paul is addressing serious problems arising out of the Corin­thians’ boastful arrogance. Since Corinth is not unique in receiving God’s Word, this church should abide by the practices “in all the churches of the saints” (v. 33).

verse_quote: does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
note: See note on 13:12 for the contrast between knowing and being known. This verse may be a warning that those who are stubborn will be disciplined by Paul or by the church (2 Thess. 3:14), but the language suggests that they will come under direct divine judgment.

These verses are a concise summary of ch. 14. The decency and orderliness of the church’s worship furthers the aim of mutual edification (vv. 3, 5, 6, 12, 14, 17, 19, 24–26, 31) and displays that our God “is not a God of confusion but of peace” (v. 33)., 40
With this verse, Paul shifts to a new topic of great concern to him—the integrity of the gospel message as it focuses on the doctrine of the resurrection.

See note on 9:27.

**believed in vain.** Denying the resurrection of Christ makes our profession of faith useless (v. 14).

These verses give the essence not only of Paul’s preaching but of the early church’s teaching as a whole (“what I also received”): Christ’s vicarious death and His resurrection as the fulfillment of the OT message (Luke 24:25–27, 45–46; 1 Pet. 1:10–11; cf. Rom. 4:23–25).

The fourfold repetition of “he appeared” indicates Paul’s emphasis in this passage—the eyewitness proof that Christ was raised from the dead (cf. Luke 1:2; 24:48; Acts 1:1–3, 21–22). Most of those who witnessed the resurrection appearances were still living at the time Paul wrote this letter, so it was possible for anyone to check the facts. Particularly significant is the reference to “more than five hundred brothers at one time,” for it shows that the appearances cannot be explained away as mere personal hallucinations.
This is not John’s brother, the apostle executed by Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:2), but the half-brother of Jesus (John 7:5; Acts 12:17; 15:13; Gal. 1:19).

This self-deprecating remark may be an ironic criticism of the Corinthians who held Paul in low esteem (2:1 note). The Gk. word rendered “one untimely born” typically refers to a miscarriage or infant born prematurely, so Paul may allude to the fact that, unlike the Twelve (including Matthias, Judas’ successor), he did not experience an extended “gestation period” of association with Jesus during His earthly ministry (cf. Acts 1:21–22). What the apostle means is suggested by the phrase “last of all.” The appearances of the risen Lord had ceased with His ascension, and Paul was a persecutor of the church when he received his calling to be an apostle (Gal. 1:13, 23; Phil. 3:6; 1 Tim. 1:13–16). Although Paul had not been with Jesus during His earthly ministry, he was granted the privilege of seeing Jesus risen from the dead, and was commissioned as the last apostle, with a special ministry to the Gentiles (Acts 9:3–5, 15; Gal. 1:15, 16). Paul strongly suggests that the apostolic office was a unique, foundational gift to the church, not one expected to continue in later generations (Eph. 2:20).

Having freely admitted the abnormal and undeserving character of his experience, Paul moves on to stress that his past life is no reason to reject his message. Where sin abounds, God’s effectual grace abounds all the more (Rom. 5:20); where we are weak, God’s grace is strong (2 Cor. 12:9, 10). Divine grace did not make Paul lazy, but caused him to labor “harder” than anyone else.

Paul finally addresses the problem that needs correction. Some of the Corinthians, perhaps without denying that Jesus had been raised, were questioning the doctrine of the resurrection because of their unbiblical understanding of the significance of the human body, or of the principles of continuity and transformation that relate our present moral body to the coming resurrection body (v. 35 note). Neo-Platonic philosophy and proto-Gnostic religious movements devalued material reality generally, including the body, and the Corinthian Christians may have been influenced by such Greco-Roman ideologies. Paul needed to show them that the resurrection of Jesus cannot be separated from the resurrection of those who are His (vv. 20–23). If their resurrection is not true, neither is His. But to deny, even by implication, that Jesus’ body was raised from the tomb destroys the message of the gospel.

verse_quote: our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
note: Cf. v. 17. The truth of the Christian message is tied to the historical reality of Christ’s death and exaltation. The apostle cannot conceive of his message as having any spiritual value if its historical foundation does not exist.

verse_quote: we are ... most to be pitied.
note: Though Paul would not deny that Christians in fact enjoy a better present life than non-Christians in many respects, this verse emphasizes that if Christ had not been raised from the dead then we ought to be pitied for our false hope. If we were still in our sins and lost (vv. 17, 18), we would have experienced the greatest and cruelest of all deceptions (vv. 31, 32). Moreover, if our hope in future resurrection is groundless, to forfeit present pleasure and endure persecution for Christ’s sake is the height of folly (vv. 30–32).

At harvest time the Israelites were required to bring an offering from the first part of the crop (Lev. 23:10). This offering was a token of the whole harvest that belonged in its entirety to God. Jesus is the “firstfruits” because His resurrection and the resurrection of believers are closely related events. Jesus was “the first to rise from the dead” incorruptible (Acts 26:23), rising as our representative. His resurrection caused us to be raised with Him by the Holy Spirit (Rom. 6:4; Eph. 2:6), and at the same time guarantees that we will be raised bodily. Another use of the metaphor is found in Rom. 8:23 (cf. also 2 Cor. 1:22; 5:5; Eph. 1:14).

This passage succinctly states one of Paul’s most profound teachings—our twofold solidarity with the first man, Adam, and with the last man, Christ. Outside of Christ, all people are by nature and by divine appointment united with Adam in sin and death; by grace and through faith, believers are united with Christ in in righteousness and in the life to come (vv. 45–49; Rom. 5:17–19). See theological note “The Last Resurrection.”
See theological note “Original Sin” on p. 17. Adam’s one sin, imputed to his posterity, results in their condemnation and death (Rom. 5:12, 15–19).

Although Paul’s argument in this section is difficult in its details, its thrust is clear and powerful. The Corinthians must understand that the resurrection is not an isolated event with limited repercussions. It is rather an integrating and culminating event in God’s sovereign rule over history. Verse 27 (“God has put all things in subjection under His feet”) is a quotation of Ps. 8:6, which speaks of an end-time ideal Adam and which has begun to find its complete realization in Christ. Redemption is not complete “until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (v. 25, a clear reference to Ps. 110:1), and since death is “the last enemy” (v. 26), Christ’s work in subduing every enemy is not complete until death is destroyed (Rev. 20:14). This final destruction of death coincides with Christ’s coming, which effects the resurrection of those who belong to Him (v. 23; see vv. 53–55). Paul’s statement that the Son “will also be subjected” to the Father (v. 28) does not mean that the Son is inferior in dignity and being. Rather, in His messianic work, the Son subjects Himself to the will of the Father “when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father” (v. 24). The climax of Christ’s submissive, messianic work is this total conquest over His enemies, “that God may be all in all,” when His absolute rule is universally acknowledged.

verse_quote: baptized on behalf of the dead.
note:
There are several interpretations of what this phrase means. Possibly, some in Corinth were being baptized on behalf of others who had already died, or, less probably, receiving baptism for the sake of reunion with believers who had died. This practice is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible or in other ancient writings. Numerous explanations of the practice have been proposed, all of them speculative and none persuasive. Some believe that Paul mentions the rite only to show the logical inconsistency of his opponents’ position. But the problem with this view is that Paul mentions “being baptized on behalf of the dead” positively, since it is based on “the dead being raised,” a point he has been making since v. 4.

A positive understanding of “being baptized on behalf of the dead” might take the reference to the “dead” as referring figuratively to Paul himself, since he says in v. 31, “I die every day,” as a reference to the suffering that his ministry entails. Paul’s suffering is mentioned immediately in vv. 30–32, and must be connected in some way with v. 29. If this interpretation is correct, then being “baptized on behalf of the dead” would mean “being baptized on behalf of Paul.” This would mean they were “being baptized _because of_ [a viable meaning of the Gk. preposition _hyper_, which the ESV renders “on behalf of”] the suffering ministry of Paul,” through which they had heard the gospel and believed and were, consequently baptized. Paul perseveres in this ministry propelled by the belief that the believing dead will be raised (cf. v. 32).

Probably a reference to Paul’s enemies in Ephesus (where this letter was written) who wanted to condemn him (cf. “the lion’s mouth,” 2 Tim. 4:17 note). One instance of potentially violent opposition against Paul was the riot stirred by the Ephesian silversmiths, although Paul’s high-placed friends, the Asiarchs, kept him from harm in that instance (Acts 19:23–41). The hope of resurrection strengthens Paul to endure severe trials and persecutions (v. 19 note).

Derived from a comedy written by the popular Greek author Menander (342–292 B.C.), this proverb was common in the ancient world (note the comparable Jewish saying in 5:6). Those Christians in Corinth with a defective view of the resurrection not only had been influenced by the bad company they kept (v. 12 note), but in their turn they were corrupting others in the congregation.

verse_quote: some have no knowledge of God.
note: Probably a reference to members of the church who boasted of their knowledge (8:1 note) but whose denial of the resurrection showed deep ignorance regarding the things of God.

verse_quote: With what kind of body do they come.
note: In this verse, Paul considers what was apparently the primary objection raised by some of the Corinthians against the future resurrection. They may have been influenced by dualism, a pagan philosophy that contrasted the immaterial with the physical and argued that the immaterial was good but the material was evil (v. 12 note). Or these Corinthians had underestimated the degree to which Christians have not yet experienced the full benefits of our redemption, including the resurrection body. Paul proceeds to argue that our present body is not the resurrection body that Christians one day will possess.

Because God created the world, the processes of nature reflect in various ways how He works. Nature provides useful metaphors and analogies of the divine work of salvation (Is. 55:10, 11). Jesus uses a seed (“if it dies, it bears much fruit”) as an illustration of the life-multiplying effect of His impending death (John 12:24). Here, Paul uses the same picture to illustrate the striking difference between what is planted and what eventually grows from the seed (v. 37). The same sort of analogy can be found in Plato’s dialogue _Symposium._ In any case, Paul’s analogy underscores the radical difference between our present bodies and our resurrection bodies, vv. 42–43.

verse_quote: to each kind of seed its own body.
note: At this point, Paul shifts the illustration to emphasize the variations among different plants. He goes on to apply the idea to living creatures (v. 39) and heavenly bodies (vv. 40, 41).

Finally, the illustration is applied to the human body that dies and is buried, and is transformed in its resurrection. Paul does not suggest that the resurrection body is a different body altogether. Just as a plant arises directly from its seed, so the resurrection body is in essence the same as the body that “is sown.” But the apostle’s emphasis is on the astounding change that will take place: from “perishable,” “dishonor,” and “weakness,” to “imperishable,” “glory,” and “power.”, 43

This last contrast is difficult to understand but is of great importance. Paul does not have in mind a contrast between physical and nonphysical, material and immaterial. The resurrection body is a physical body, not an intangible ghost. The apostle has already used the words “natural” and “spiritual” to distinguish the individual who does not have the Holy Spirit from the one who does (2:6, 14 notes). The natural person belongs to the present age (1:20), while the spiritual person is a citizen of heaven (Phil. 3:20). Christians have received the Holy Spirit and are on that account “spiritual.” They have not yet received the spiritual “body,” the physical body that will be fully conformed to the life given by the Spirit. See Rom. 8:22–25 and note.

Paul clarifies his meaning by continuing the contrast between the first and the last Adam (vv. 21, 22 note). The Gk. word translated “being” (_psychē_) is related to the word translated “natural” in v. 44 (_psychikos_), while the word “spirit” (_pneuma_) corresponds to “spiritual” (_pneumatikos_). The words “life-giving spirit” are most probably a reference to the Holy Spirit. Jesus and the Holy Spirit share the same divine essence but are not the same divine person, but Christ and the Spirit are identified in terms of their presence and activity in the church. This identity, known to us because Jesus, too, is life-giving, is the fulfillment of Jesus’ role as Messiah and commenced with His resurrection and ascension. To be in Christ is to be in the Spirit also (6:11, 15, 19; 12:11). The association of Christ, the Holy Spirit, and life is apparent in Rom. 8:9–11 and 2 Cor. 3:6, 17, 18. By citing and supplementing Gen. 2:7, Paul shows that Adam, even at his creation and before sin, did not possess and could not have conferred on his descendants the Spirit-empowered life of the age to come. Only the last Adam, Christ, can give others eternal life through His Spirit. The physically life-giving breath that the first Adam received foreshadowed typologically the “life-giving Spirit” that Christ, “the last Adam,” would give to His people, as a result of His own resurrection. The apparent point is that the first human was created to reach the goal of such a glorious, imperishable body, _if_ he had obeyed God and been faithful in reflecting God’s image. In contrast to the first Adam, who failed because of faithless disobedience, Christ has subdued and obeyed in the way His progenitor should have. Consequently, Christ has inherited that for which humanity was originally destined but failed to reach. Jesus’ body was not only a renewed physical body, but it had become “heavenly,” “spiritual,” and “imperishable.”

Here is a final contrast, suggesting that vv. 42–44 refer to the distinction between earthly and heavenly human bodies. In this context, however, the distinction is not one of substance but of time; the present evil age is contrasted with the coming perfect age. Believers already enjoy some of the blessings of the coming age (10:11 note) but still await its consummation. God’s work of redemption will not be complete until the bodily resurrection. We have borne the image of the first Adam, and since we belong to Christ, we are destined to bear the image of the last Adam, namely, Christ Himself (v. 49).

This phrase alludes to the weakness of earthly, human existence and is an equivalent to “perishable.” Paul is warning the Co­rinthians that without new “imperishable” bodies, we “cannot inherit the kingdom of God.” How, then, can some deny the doctrine of the resurrection?

See note on 2:7. For Paul, “mystery” is not an impenetrable paradox but a truth once partially hidden by God and now revealed in the gospel of Christ (Rom. 16:25–26; Eph. 3:3–9). The fuller truth revealed here in vv. 51–55 is about what will happen to _living_ believers (those who do not “sleep,” v. 51) when the resurrection of the dead occurs. Nowhere in the OT was it made clear that at this time living believers will be transformed along with dead ones, so that all will be changed into imperishable and immortal resurrection bodies.

**We shall not all sleep.** Paul recognizes that many Christians will not die but will be alive at the time of Christ’s return. Though these Christians will not be raised from death, they will also be transformed and receive imperishable and immortal bodies (1 Thess. 4:13–18 and notes).

This is one of the most eloquent and powerful passages in Scripture. With paraphrases of Isaiah and Hosea (based on the Septuagint), Paul alludes to his earlier argument in vv. 24–28 and vigorously assures us of the finality of death’s destruction on the day of resurrection. This day will also mark the destruction of “sin” and “the law” as the instrument of sin. In the letter to the Romans, Paul explains in detail how sin is the venom bringing death to all (Rom. 5:12) and how the law, though itself holy, becomes an instrument through which sin can deceive (Rom. 7:7–12).

In the face of false teaching and various temptations, the hope of the resurrection should encourage the Corinthians to persevere in their faith. The exhortation to be “immovable,” however, does not imply inactivity. On the contrary, the Corinthians must be fully active in “the work of the Lord.” We can become easily discouraged by thinking that our labor may come to nothing (Gal. 2:2; Phil. 2:16; 1 Thess. 3:5), but we can remember the promise that when God creates the new heavens and new earth, His people will enjoy the fruits of their toil, and see that their efforts were never “in vain” (Is. 65:17–25).

From Rom. 15:25–27 and 2 Cor. 8:1–15, it appears that one of the purposes of Paul’s third missionary journey was to raise an offering from the Gentiles for Jewish Christians in Judea who were in need, possibly as a result of persecution. Apparently, Paul had already told the Corinthians about this project in an earlier letter, in which he also addressed other issues (5:9). They had asked for more information, and Paul proceeds to give directions about taking up the collection (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**for the saints.** See note on 1:2. As in 2 Cor. 8:4; 9:1, here Paul has in view specifically the followers of Jesus residing in Judea, from whom the gospel went out to the Gentiles (Rom. 15:26–27).

verse_quote: On the first day of every week.
note: The reference is to Sunday, the day on which the resurrected Lord met with His disciples (John 20:19, 26; cf. also “the Lord’s day” in Rev. 1:10). Acts 20:7 indicates that the early Christians met on Sunday “to break bread” (part of their worship), and it would have been appropriate also to designate that day for collecting the offering in worship.

This comment possibly reflects doubts on the part of some as to whether Paul should be given sole responsibility for the money (2:1 note). In 2 Cor. 8:16–24, Paul emphasizes the full trustworthiness of Titus and one or more other brothers appointed by the churches themselves to administer the reception and transmission of this offering, to enlist the Corinthians’ confidence that their gift will reach its intended destination (see Acts 20:4).

These verses make clear that Paul wrote the letter from Ephesus and intended to visit Corinth by way of the northern land route around the Aegean Sea. Both Acts 20:1, 2 and 2 Cor. 2:12, 13 indicate that he carried out this plan. What Paul did not foresee at this time was the prior need to make a short and unpleasant visit to Corinth soon after writing 1 Corinthians (2 Cor. 1:23; 2:1; 13:2; cf. Introduction to 2 Corinthians: Date and Occasion).
Paul’s resolve to prolong his ministry in Ephesus until Pentecost was determined by the opportunity for fruitful gospel labor in the city, despite the many opponents arrayed against him (15:32).

Earlier (4:17), Paul mentioned that Timothy was coming as his representative (Acts 19:22). Paul wants them to treat his younger coworker with respect and kindness—in contrast to the criticism that some in the Corinthian church lodged against Paul himself.

Apparently, the Corinthians in their letter had asked for Apollos to return to them (Introduction: Date and Occasion; Acts 18:27–19:1). In spite of the improper attitude of the Corinthians (4:6; 4:15 note), Paul honored their request. It was not Apollos’s “will” to go at this time, but he would come later. Thus, this brief report reinforces Paul’s earlier affirmation that he and Apollos are not competitors but co-laborers with mutual respect for each other’s distinctive ministries (3:4–11).

This passage commends “Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus,” who probably had carried the letter from the church in Corinth. Paul’s emphasis (especially in the words “I urge you, brothers ... be subject”) suggests that these men, Stephanas in particular, were appointed leaders but did not enjoy proper respect from the congregation (cf. 1:16). The phrase “for your absence” does not necessarily imply a criticism (the Greek at the end of Phil. 2:30 is almost identical), but here it may suggest that the church as a whole failed to refresh his spirit.

Ephesus, where 1 Corinthians was written, was the most important city in the Roman province of Asia, the southwestern part of the Anatolian peninsula, which is today part of modern Turkey (Acts 19:10).

**Aquila and Prisca.** This couple played an important role during Paul’s initial visit to Corinth (Acts 18:1–3), so the congregation knew them well. They accompanied Paul from Corinth as far as Ephesus (Acts 18:18–19, 26), and thus were reunited with the apostle when he returned to that Asian metropolis (19:1). By the time he wrote to the church at Rome from Corinth, Prisca and Aquila had returned to Rome, from which an imperial edict had previously expelled them and other Jews, and were hosting a church in their home (Rom. 16:3–5) as they had done in Ephesus and probably elsewhere.

A normal greeting in the early church. Though this practice was not uncommon in Judaism and Roman culture, the word “holy” indicates the added significance such a greeting had among the saints, since it represented the special relationship of brothers and sisters in Christ (Rom. 16:16 note; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14).

Like some of Paul’s other epistles, the letter up to this point would have been written by a trained scribe (Rom. 16:22), but Paul’s custom was to add a few words himself as a personal signature (see Gal. 6:11; 2 Thess. 3:17).

These strong words, written in Paul’s own hand, assert the apostolic authority behind the whole letter. This is not a curse on unbelievers in general but on those who reject the authority of the letter (14:37; Gal. 1:8, 9; 2 Thess. 3:14, 15).

**Our Lord, come.** Paul gives a transliteration of the Aramaic words _Marana tha_ (or _Maran atha,_ “Our Lord has come”), reflecting the worship of the early church in Palestine. The phrase reflects the universal Christian desire for the Lord Jesus Christ to return in glory and to complete the work of salvation now begun in believers (Rev. 22:20).

verse_quote: My love be with you all.
note: After a long letter consisting primarily of severe rebukes, these affectionate words may come as a surprise. Paul has not forgotten the pastoral needs of his congregation (1:2 note).
